Medical Brain / GHS402 / Microbiology

Ky's GHS402 Microbiology Study Guide

Gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary microbiology from the GHS402 lecture decks, one section per lecture group. Every fact is taken from the slides.

1. HSV-1, Norovirus and Rotavirus

Lecture scope: Lecture 1: herpes simplex virus type 1, rotavirus and norovirus.

Slide decks: Lect 1, HSV-1, Norovirus, Rotavirus (15 Qs)

Herpes simplex virus 1 infects mucoepithelial cells, causes disease at the site of contact, then becomes latent in a sensory ganglion, so recurrences return to the same site, set off by ultraviolet light, fever, stress, menstruation or immunosuppression; resolution needs cell-mediated immunity, since the virus spreads from cell to cell and avoids antibody. The latent site is the trigeminal ganglia for HSV-1 and the sacral ganglia for HSV-2, and acyclovir, famciclovir or valacyclovir have no effect on latency.

The herpes syndromes are told apart by the patient or setting. Gingivostomatitis is a severe primary infection of children 1 to 6 years, herpetic pharyngotonsillitis is primary infection in adults, and herpes labialis is a recurrent infection of adults at the vermilion border. Herpetic whitlow, a throbbing swollen finger, is seen in nurses, physicians, thumb-suckers and people with genital HSV, herpes gladiatorum belongs to wrestlers and rugby players, and eczema herpeticum, in children with active atopic dermatitis, is an emergency treated with acyclovir. A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells and Cowdry A inclusions but is non-specific.

Rotavirus and norovirus injure the small intestinal lining directly and cause a self-limited watery diarrhea, separated by patient (an infant or an outbreak), season and test. Rotavirus is seen in infants and daycare and is diagnosed by stool antigen ELISA; norovirus causes outbreaks on cruise ships, in schools, camps and hospitals, and is diagnosed by RT-PCR.

High-Yield Notes

Read the table below one syndrome at a time: the middle column gives the patient or setting that names the syndrome, and the last column gives the clue that goes with it. Herpetic pharyngotonsillitis and herpes labialis are separated in the middle column as primary against recurrent infection of adults, and for keratoconjunctivitis that column holds how many eyes are involved rather than a kind of patient.

SyndromePatient or settingClue
GingivostomatitisChildren 1 to 6 yearsFever, irritability, cervical nodes, painful oral vesicles; severe primary infection
Herpetic pharyngotonsillitisAdults, primary infectionVesicles in the pharynx and tonsils
Herpes labialisRecurrent infection of adultsTingling, then crops of vesicles at the vermilion border; same site each time
KeratoconjunctivitisAlmost always one eyeCorneal ulcers; recurrences scar the cornea and can blind
Herpetic whitlowNurses, physicians, thumb-suckers, people with genital HSVThrobbing, swollen finger with vesicles
Herpes gladiatorumWrestlers and rugby playersClustered vesicles on trunk, arms, face or neck; flu-like illness and nodes
Eczema herpeticumChildren with active atopic dermatitisPunched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crust; emergency, treat with acyclovir

The two intestinal viruses compared. In genome, rotavirus is segmented dsRNA with 11 segments and a double-layered capsid, and norovirus is single-stranded positive-sense RNA, non-enveloped. In who and when, rotavirus is seen in infants and daycare, in winter, and is the commonest childhood diarrhea worldwide; norovirus is highly contagious, can infect anyone and causes outbreaks on cruise ships, in schools, camps and hospitals, and is the winter vomiting bug. Incubation is 1 to 3 days for rotavirus and 12 to 48 hours for norovirus.

The injury of rotavirus is villous atrophy with impaired sodium absorption and potassium loss; the injury of norovirus is microvillous damage, apoptosis and loss of tight junction proteins. Diagnosis is by stool antigen ELISA for rotavirus and by RT-PCR for norovirus. Under prevention, rotavirus has oral live vaccines, and norovirus resists chlorine, alcohol, vinegar, heat and freezing.

For HSV, a Tzanck smear from the base of the vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells and eosinophilic Cowdry A inclusions, but it is non-specific; direct immunofluorescent antibody staining and viral culture are the other tests. Acyclovir, famciclovir or valacyclovir inhibit viral DNA polymerase and terminate the chain, with IV acyclovir for the immunocompromised or for encephalitis and topical penciclovir or acyclovir second line. None of them has any effect on latency.

Points that carry questions
  • HSV-1 sits in the trigeminal ganglia and HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia; genital lesions below the waist are usually HSV-2, and erythema multiforme can follow HSV-1.
  • Rotarix is live attenuated (G1) in 2 doses at 2 and 4 months; RotaTeq is a live reassortant with a human outer protein in a bovine strain in 3 doses at 2, 4 and 6 months; both are contraindicated after intussusception.

2. Protozoa Causing Diarrhea

Lecture scope: Lecture 2: intestinal protozoa (Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora and Cyclospora): stages, pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment.

Slide decks: Lect 2, Protozoa causing diarrhea (20 Qs)

Five protozoa cause the diarrheas of this lecture, and all five are swallowed as cysts or oocysts in fecally contaminated food or water. Entamoeba histolytica invades the colon: its trophozoite secretes enzymes that cause localized necrosis with little inflammation, and it then reaches the liver through the portal circulation, which is why it is the only one that makes bloody dysentery and a liver abscess. In the stool, amebic dysentery shows few inflammatory cells, whereas bacillary dysentery shows many polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

Giardia lamblia sits on the duodenal wall and does not invade or enter the blood; its diarrhea is watery, foul-smelling and non-bloody, with no fever. Cryptosporidium, Cystoisospora and Cyclospora are the oocyst formers, told apart by exposure and host: Cryptosporidium has pools and lakes as its setting and is mild in immunocompetent patients but severe in AIDS, Cystoisospora causes chronic profuse diarrhea in immunocompromised patients, and Cyclospora follows raspberries or contaminated water in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients.

Treatment of Entamoeba follows the stage: a tissue agent (metronidazole or tinidazole) for symptomatic disease and a luminal agent (iodoquinol or paromomycin) for the asymptomatic cyst passer.

High-Yield Notes

Read the table below one organism at a time: each row gives the clinical picture and setting that names the organism, how it is diagnosed, and the drug that treats it. The diagnosis column carries its own discriminations, because an ingested red cell means Entamoeba, a suction disk means Giardia, and oocysts on a modified acid-fast stain are how Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora are found.

OrganismClinical picture and settingDiagnosisTreatment
Entamoeba histolyticaDysentery (bloody, mucus-containing), tenesmus, flatulence; liver abscess with RUQ pain, fever and tender liver; ameboma mimics colon cancer; anal-oral spread; no animal reservoirTrophozoites with ingested red cells in diarrheal stool; cysts with up to 4 nuclei in formed stool; three specimens; serology for invasive diseaseMetronidazole or tinidazole; iodoquinol or paromomycin for asymptomatic carriers
Giardia lambliaWatery, foul-smelling, non-bloody diarrhea with bloating and cramps for weeks, no fever; hikers, day care, IgA deficiency; mammal reservoirsTrophozoite attaches by a suction disk; trophozoites or cysts in diarrheal stool; stool antigen ELISA; string test if negativeTinidazole (better tolerated) or metronidazole
Cryptosporidium hominisWatery diarrhea, mild if immunocompetent, severe in AIDS; jejunum; pools and lakesOocysts on modified Kinyoun acid-fast stain; stool antigenNitazoxanide; paromomycin may help in AIDS
Cystoisospora (Isospora) belliChronic profuse diarrhea in immunocompromised patients; invades upper small intestine and destroys the brush borderOocysts in fecal specimensTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; clindamycin if resistant
Cyclospora cayetanensisProlonged, relapsing watery diarrhea in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients; raspberries and contaminated waterSpherical oocysts on modified acid-fast stainTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

Entamoeba and Giardia are the two organisms taught by stage. The cyst of Entamoeba histolytica has four nuclei, is killed by boiling but not by chlorination, and is removed by filtration; the cyst of Giardia lamblia is likewise not killed by chlorination and is removed by filtration. Entamoeba has a motile trophozoite and a nonmotile cyst. The Entamoeba trophozoite has a single nucleus, even peripheral chromatin and a central karyosome, and eats red cells; the Giardia trophozoite is pear-shaped, with two nuclei, four pairs of flagella and a suction disk.

In site and behavior, Entamoeba is in the ileum, then colonizes the cecum and colon, and invades to portal blood and liver: a lesion that reaches the muscularis forms the flask-shaped ulcer, and progression into the submucosa leads to portal invasion. Its antibodies are not protective, since previous infection does not prevent reinfection, but they serve serologic diagnosis. Amebiasis and giardiasis are both common in male homosexuals, giardiasis through oral-anal contact. Giardia excysts in the duodenum and does not invade or enter blood; its stool is watery, not bloody. The Entamoeba stool is bloody and mucoid with few inflammatory cells, whereas bacillary dysentery has many polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

The drugs on the slides are told apart by mechanism. Metronidazole disrupts the DNA of microbial cells and inhibits nucleic acid synthesis. Paromomycin is a protein synthesis inhibitor binding 16S ribosomal RNA. Nitazoxanide inhibits pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase in anaerobic energy metabolism. Albendazole inhibits tubulin polymerization, impairing glucose uptake and depleting glycogen. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole disrupts folate synthesis, so thymidine and nucleotide supply fails.

Points that carry questions
  • Liver abscess pus is brownish-yellow with the consistency of anchovy paste (reddish-brown in the slide 26 photograph), and it need not be drained; about 90% of infections are asymptomatic.
  • Diarrheal stool is examined within 1 hour to see trophozoite motility, and the commonest error is mistaking fecal leukocytes for trophozoites.
  • Trichomonas is the only protozoan in the overview that is spread sexually; it has no cyst and its trophozoite causes vaginal discharge.

3. Peritonitis, Lumpy Jaw and H. pylori

Lecture scope: Lecture 3: Actinomyces israelii (lumpy jaw and other forms) and Bacteroides fragilis (abscess, peritonitis, diverticulitis): pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention. Plus the school SGD on anaerobes, Actinomyces and Helicobacter pylori (self study): organism features, urease, CagA, disease associations and treatment.

Slide decks: Lect 3, Peritonitis, Lumpy jaw (11 Qs) · SGD, Anaerobes, Actinomyces, H. pylori (pre-reading) (7 Qs)

Actinomyces israelii is a Gram-positive branching filamentous member of the normal flora that is not communicable and causes disease only when trauma or surgery breaks the mucosal barrier, giving swelling, draining sinus tracts and hard yellow "sulfur" granules. Bacteroides fragilis is colonic flora that causes abdominal abscesses, peritonitis and diverticulitis when bowel defects, surgery or trauma spill it into sterile sites. Anaerobic infection is suggested by foul-smelling discharge, proximity to a mucosal surface, gas in tissues and negative aerobic cultures.

The treatment split is the point to remember: penicillin G for actinomycosis, and metronidazole or clindamycin plus drainage for Bacteroides. In the laboratory, Actinomyces israelii shows Gram-positive branching bacilli in granules and its anaerobic culture gives molar tooth colonies, and Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobic Gram-negative rod that is bile tolerant, has a polysaccharide capsule and is black on bile-esculin agar with gentamicin.

Helicobacter pylori is a curved or spiral Gram-negative motile rod that is urease positive and colonizes the gastric antrum. Its clinical picture is chronic gastritis, duodenal ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma, and its treatment is triple therapy.

High-Yield Notes

The table below holds the organisms of the lecture, with the clue, laboratory feature and treatment for each. Read it one row at a time, from the setting and clinical picture to the laboratory column and then the treatment column. The rows for Peptostreptococcus and Clostridium and for Escherichia coli and Enterococcus describe mixed infection with Bacteroides, and the Actinomyces odontolyticus row gives the treatment of actinomycosis in its treatment cell.

OrganismSetting and clinical pictureLaboratoryTreatment
Actinomyces israeliiEndogenous (skin, oropharynx, GIT, vagina); invasive growth in tissues with low oxygenation; lumpy jaw after dental trauma or extraction; draining abscesses with sulfur granulesGram-positive branching bacilli in granules; anaerobic culture gives molar tooth coloniesPenicillin G, then penicillin V; surgical drainage
Actinomyces odontolyticusActinomyces species named only for its colony colorRust-brown or red coloniesActinomycosis is treated with penicillin G
Bacteroides fragilisColonic flora; abscesses, peritonitis, diverticulitis; also synergistic myonecrosisAnaerobic Gram-negative rod; bile tolerant; polysaccharide capsule; black on bile-esculin agar with gentamicinMetronidazole or clindamycin; drain abscesses

The site of actinomycosis follows the route of the break in the barrier. By form and predisposition, cervicofacial (lumpy jaw) actinomycosis is listed with dental trauma or poor oral hygiene, pelvic with intrauterine contraceptive devices, abdominal with surgery or bowel trauma, and thoracic with aspiration of oral secretions. The CNS form is listed with a solitary brain abscess, and keratoactinomycosis with the cornea.

The drugs named in the lecture, and what each is for, are these. Penicillin G is the drug of choice for actinomycosis, parenteral for 4 to 6 weeks. Penicillin V is the oral follow-on for weeks to months. Metronidazole and clindamycin are the treatment of Bacteroides and other anaerobic infection. Cefoxitin is prophylaxis before GIT or biliary tract surgery. Gentamicin is added to bile-esculin medium; B. fragilis is resistant, most other bacteria are inhibited.

The table below gives the virulence factors and preventive measures from the school SGD on these organisms. Read across a row from the virulence factor to the key feature and then to the regimen or prevention. For Actinomyces israelii the virulence factor is not stated. The last column mixes treatment and prevention: in the Bacteroides fragilis cell, cefoxitin before GI surgery is the prevention and metronidazole or clindamycin is the treatment.

OrganismVirulence factorKey featureRegimen or prevention
Bacteroides fragilisPolysaccharide capsule, which allows abscess formationBile tolerant; reduced endotoxin activityCefoxitin before GI surgery; metronidazole or clindamycin
Actinomyces israeliiNot statedEndogenous; needs mucosal disruption; draining sinus tracts with sulfur granulesLong-term penicillin G plus surgical drainage

Points that carry questions
  • Foul smell comes from short-chain fatty acids made by anaerobic metabolism, and gas in tissue is fermentation.
  • Diverticulitis gives left lower quadrant pain with a mass, fever, and constipation or diarrhea.
  • Peritonitis features fever and rebound tenderness, and abscess pus is foul and poorly walled off.

4. Intestinal Helminths: Cestodes

Lecture scope: Lecture 4a: medically important tapeworms (Taenia solium, Taenia saginata, Diphyllobothrium latum, Echinococcus granulosus): life cycles, taeniasis versus cysticercosis, hydatid disease, diagnosis and treatment.

Slide decks: Lect 4a, Intestinal Helminths, Cestodes (20 Qs)

Tapeworms are flat, segmented worms with a scolex that anchors to the gut wall and a chain of proglottids whose gravid segments shed eggs in the stool. The exam turns on which stage a person swallows: larvae in undercooked pork, beef or fish give an intestinal adult that causes little damage, whereas swallowed eggs give the dangerous tissue diseases, cysticercosis (eggs from human feces, not from pork) and hydatid disease (eggs shed by dogs).

Among the intestinal adults, the two Taenia are told apart by the scolex or the gravid proglottids, and D. latum has a scolex of its own. Taenia solium has four suckers and a circle of hooks, and proglottids with 5 to 10 primary uterine branches; Taenia saginata has four suckers and no hooklets, 15 to 20 uterine branches, and never causes cysticercosis; Diphyllobothrium latum has two sucking grooves and no hooks. The stool egg is a trap: the eggs of T. solium, T. saginata and Echinococcus are identical, and the species is named from the worm, not the egg, whereas the oval operculated egg of D. latum is itself diagnostic.

Praziquantel is used for the intestinal tapeworms and is also an option for cysticercosis, whereas albendazole is named for neurocysticercosis and for the hydatid cyst of Echinococcus granulosus, with or without surgical removal.

High-Yield Notes

Read the table below one tapeworm at a time: the four medically important tapeworms are told apart by what is swallowed, where the worm lives and what the stool shows, and the last column gives the treatment where one is given. Taenia solium has a row for taeniasis and a row for cysticercosis, and Hymenolepis nana is on the last row, named on the slides only as a cestode of minor importance.

CestodeAcquired byHost and siteDiagnosisTreatment
Taenia solium (pork tapeworm), taeniasisLarvae (cysticerci) in undercooked pork; pigs reach human feces; endemic in Asia, South America and Eastern Europe, and most US cases are imported; about 3 months to reach adultHuman definitive host, pig intermediate (pigs infected by eating vegetation contaminated with eggs or gravid proglottids; cysticerci in muscle are the infective stage); adult in intestine, up to 5 m; scolex with four suckers and a circle of hooksEggs or gravid proglottids in feces are the diagnostic stage; proglottids with 5 to 10 primary uterine branches; eggs found less oftenPraziquantel
Taenia solium, cysticercosisEggs in food or water contaminated with human feces; autoinfection possibleCysticerci in brain, eyes, skin and muscle; living cysts cause no inflammation, dead ones do, then calcifyCyst on biopsy or CT; ELISA may be negative in neurocysticercosisAlbendazole for neurocysticercosis, or praziquantel; surgical excision may be needed
Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm)Larvae in undercooked beefHuman definitive host, cattle intermediate (infected the same way as pigs); intestine, up to 10 m; four suckers, no hooklets; never causes cysticercosisGravid proglottids with 15 to 20 uterine branches in stoolPraziquantel
Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm)Plerocercoid larvae in raw freshwater fishHuman definitive host; eggs must reach fresh water, then copepods (procercoid larvae) and fish (plerocercoid or sparganum larvae) are the two intermediate hosts; longest tapeworm, up to 13 m; scolex with two sucking grooves and no hooksOval operculated eggs in stool; no serologic testPraziquantel
Echinococcus granulosus (dog tapeworm)Embryonated eggs (the infective stage) in food contaminated with dog fecesDogs and other canines definitive; sheep, goats and swine intermediate; human accidental; adult has hooks on an armed rostellum; unilocular hydatid cyst in liver, lung, brain and bone; one of the smallest tapeworms (scolex and only three proglottids)Brood capsules with protoscoleces on microscopy; serology such as indirect hemagglutination; CTAlbendazole with or without surgical removal
Hymenolepis nanaNamed on the slides only as a cestode of minor importanceNo further features are givenNot givenNot given

The stool egg is a trap: the species is not named from it. In appearance, the egg of Taenia solium, T. saginata and Echinococcus is small and round, with a thick radially striated shell and an embryo with three pairs of hooklets, and it is identical in the three; what names the species is the worm, by its gravid proglottids (uterine branches) or scolex, not the egg. The egg of Diphyllobothrium latum is an oval operculated egg, and there the egg itself is diagnostic.

The table below sorts which drug fits which worm. Read across each row from the drug or agent to what it is used for, and then to the point to know about it: for praziquantel that point is its action on the worm muscle, for albendazole it is the diseases it is named for, and for ethanol or hypertonic saline it is what the injection does. What each disease does to the patient is in the box that follows.

Drug or agentUsed forPoint to know
PraziquantelIntestinal tapeworms (T. solium, T. saginata, D. latum); also an option for cysticercosisCauses spasm and paralysis of the worm muscle with rapid Ca2+ influx
AlbendazoleNeurocysticercosis; hydatid cyst (E. granulosus)Named for neurocysticercosis (slide 35) and hydatid cyst (slide 53)
Ethanol or hypertonic salineInjected into a hydatid cyst before removalProtoscolicidal: kills the organisms and prevents accidental dissemination
Points that carry questions
  • D. latum can cause megaloblastic anemia by vitamin B12 deficiency, because the worm preferentially takes up the vitamin.
  • Motile T. saginata proglottids may protrude from the anus and cause pruritus ani.
  • Hydatid liver cysts may cause hepatic dysfunction, lung cysts can erode into a bronchus with bloody sputum, and cerebral cysts cause headache and focal neurologic signs.
  • Hydatid cyst rupture, spontaneous or at trauma or surgery, can cause fatal anaphylactic shock and spreads protoscoleces.
  • Neurocysticercosis causes headache, vomiting and seizures; in the eye it causes uveitis, retinitis or a larva floating in the vitreous.

5. Intestinal Helminths: Trematodes

Lecture scope: Lecture 4b: medically important flukes (Schistosoma mansoni, japonicum and haematobium, Clonorchis sinensis, Paragonimus westermani): life cycles, egg morphology, pathogenesis, clinical stages, diagnosis and praziquantel treatment.

Slide decks: Lect 4b, Intestinal Helminths, Trematodes (17 Qs)

Three flukes matter medically: Schistosoma (blood flukes), Clonorchis sinensis (liver fluke) and Paragonimus westermani (lung fluke), remembered as Sweet Cheese Pie. Humans are the definitive host (sexual cycle) and freshwater snails the intermediate host (asexual multiplication). Schistosomes send free-swimming cercariae through the skin, whereas Clonorchis and Paragonimus arrive as cysts in raw fish or crab, and in schistosomiasis the damage comes from the eggs, not the adults, while hepatocytes stay undamaged.

The three schistosomes are told apart by the egg. Schistosoma mansoni lives in the veins of the colon, and its egg has a large lateral spine and is found in stool. Schistosoma japonicum also has its egg in stool, with a very small lateral spine, and is found in Asia only, with domestic animals (water buffalo, pigs) as reservoirs. Schistosoma haematobium lives in the veins of the urinary bladder, and its egg has a large terminal spine and is found in urine. Clonorchis sinensis is acquired from raw or undercooked fish and lives in the biliary ducts, whereas Paragonimus westermani is acquired from raw or undercooked crab and lives in the lung; the Clonorchis egg and the Paragonimus egg are operculated.

Swimmer's itch (cercarial dermatitis) must not be confused with the real disease. It appears minutes to hours after exposure as immediate IgE-mediated papules to non-human schistosome cercariae in skin, with no replication in humans and no disseminated disease. Acute schistosomiasis is itch and dermatitis, then fever, chills, diarrhea, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly 2 to 3 weeks later, with eosinophilia to migrating larvae, and it usually resolves spontaneously. In chronic S. mansoni or S. japonicum infection most patients are asymptomatic; egg granulomas give GI hemorrhage, hepatomegaly, massive splenomegaly and portal hypertension, and death is most often from ruptured esophageal varices.

High-Yield Notes

Read the table below one fluke at a time. The five flukes are told apart by route of infection, where the adult lives, the egg and the region, and the adult site column also names the hosts. The schistosome rows are acquired when cercariae penetrate skin, whereas the Clonorchis row is acquired as larvae in raw or undercooked fish and the Paragonimus row as larvae in raw or undercooked crab. The treatment column reads praziquantel in all five rows.

FlukeAcquired byAdult site and hostsEggRegionTreatment

The three schistosomes are told apart by the egg, so read the spine: its size, its position and the specimen it turns up in (Lect 4b, slides 13 and 19; class notes, trematodes, 6 Oct 2026). SpeciesSpine on the eggSpecimenTrap to avoid

Schistosomiasis passes through a skin phase, an acute phase and a chronic phase, and swimmer's itch must not be confused with the real disease. Read the timing column first: swimmer's itch appears minutes to hours after exposure, whereas in acute schistosomiasis the fever and the other findings come 2 to 3 weeks later than the itch and dermatitis. The chronic rows, including clonorchiasis, are those where most patients are asymptomatic, and the last column gives the cause and findings.

PresentationTimingCause and findings
Swimmer's itch (cercarial dermatitis)Minutes to hours after exposureNon-human schistosome cercariae in skin; immediate IgE-mediated papules; no replication in humans and no disseminated disease
Acute schistosomiasisItch and dermatitis, then fever, chills, diarrhea, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly 2 to 3 weeks laterEosinophilia to migrating larvae; usually resolves spontaneously
Chronic S. mansoni or S. japonicumMost patients asymptomaticEgg granulomas give GI hemorrhage, hepatomegaly, massive splenomegaly and portal hypertension; death is most often from ruptured esophageal varices
Clonorchiasis, heavy burdenChronic; most patients asymptomaticUpper abdominal pain, anorexia, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia; biliary hyperplasia, fibrosis, pigmented gallstones and cholangiocarcinoma

The stages of the schistosome cycle in order, from the egg to the human blood, each with its host and place and the point to know. The miracidium hatches from eggs in fresh water and penetrates snail tissue; it infects the snail, not humans. The sporocyst is inside the snail and releases cercariae back into the water. The cercaria is free-swimming in water, is fork-tailed, is the infective stage and penetrates human skin. The schistosomulum is in the blood, then portal blood to the liver: cercariae lose their tails during penetration and become schistosomulae, and mature into adults in the liver.

Points that carry questions
  • Adult schistosomes have separate sexes and the female lies in the male's gynecophoric canal; the other trematodes are hermaphrodites.
  • Diagnosis is by eggs in stool or urine, and the deck says serologic tests are not useful, including in clonorchiasis. Standard teaching does use serology in returning travellers and early infection before eggs appear, though it cannot separate active from past infection.
  • These flukes are not endemic in the United States, but immigrants from tropical areas, especially Southeast Asia, are frequently infected.
  • Schistosomes evade immunity by coating themselves with host antigens; liver function tests stay normal.
  • Prevention: proper disposal of human waste, snail eradication and no swimming in endemic water; for Clonorchis, thorough cooking of fish.

6. Intestinal Helminths: Nematodes

Lecture scope: Lecture 5 and SGD: intestinal nematodes (Enterobius, Trichuris, Ascaris, hookworms, Strongyloides) and larval tissue disease (cutaneous larva migrans, Toxocara): infective stage, life cycle, pathology, diagnosis and treatment.

Slide decks: Lect 5, Intestinal Helminths, Nematodes (21 Qs) · SGD, Nematodes (5 Qs)

Nematodes are roundworms with a cylindrical body, a complete digestive tract (mouth and anus) and separate sexes. The intestinal nematodes are remembered as ETANeST: Enterobius, Trichuris, Ascaris, Necator and Ancylostoma, Strongyloides and Trichinella. The exam question is how the person was infected: Enterobius, Trichuris, Ascaris and Toxocara arrive as swallowed eggs, while Strongyloides and the hookworms arrive as larvae that penetrate the skin.

The diagnosis turns on what is found and where. Enterobius eggs are not in stool and are recovered by Scotch tape on perianal skin; Trichuris, Ascaris and the hookworms are found as eggs in stool; Strongyloides shows rhabditiform larvae, not eggs, in stool. Among the worms that penetrate the skin, the hookworms cause microcytic anemia from blood loss, whereas Strongyloides has autoinfection, with hyperinfection with enteric sepsis when immunosuppressed. In Trichuris, anemia is less marked than in hookworm, though heavy infection can cause it, and heavy childhood infection brings rectal prolapse.

Tissue-migrating nematodes cause marked eosinophilia, through IL-4 (IgE) and IL-5 (eosinophils) from Th2 cells; eosinophils kill by attaching to the worm through IgE and releasing granule enzymes. The larval conditions are a separate discrimination: ground itch is human hookworm larvae entering the skin, cutaneous larva migrans is Ancylostoma caninum (dog) and A. braziliense (cat), whose larvae cannot complete their cycle in humans, and visceral larva migrans is Toxocara canis, with humans as dead-end hosts after ingesting soil eggs.

High-Yield Notes

The table below tells the intestinal nematodes apart by how they are acquired, what they do and how they are found and treated; read it one worm at a time. For the first five worms, the acquired-by column separates ingested eggs from filariform larvae that penetrate the skin, and the diagnosis column carries the egg shapes, together with Enterobius, whose eggs are not in stool, and Strongyloides, found as rhabditiform larvae. The row for Trichinella carries its ETANeST listing and the parasite hint list features, and its diagnosis and treatment are not stated.

OrganismAcquired byKey clinical featureDiagnosisTreatment

TrichinellaListed in ETANeSTMyalgias and periorbital edema (parasite hint list)Not statedNot stated

Larval disease is easily confused between the hookworm rash, the dog and cat hookworm track and the Toxocara syndrome. Read the table below across each row: the cause and host column names whose larvae are responsible, the findings column gives what is seen, and the last column gives diagnosis and treatment. For ground itch that column says to treat the hookworm infection, while the cutaneous and visceral larva migrans rows name drugs, with no proven treatment for the visceral form.

ConditionCause and hostFindingsDiagnosis and treatment
Ground itchHuman hookworm larvae entering the skinPruritic papule or vesicle at the site of entryTreat the hookworm infection
Cutaneous larva migrans (creeping eruption)Ancylostoma caninum (dog) and A. braziliense (cat); larvae cannot complete their cycle in humansExtremely pruritic serpiginous track; southern United States, children and construction workersClinical diagnosis; albendazole or ivermectin
Visceral larva migransToxocara canis; dog is definitive host; humans are dead-end hosts after ingesting soil eggsGranulomas to dead larvae (delayed hypersensitivity) in liver, brain, eyes; fever, hepatomegaly, eosinophilia, hypergammaglobulinemia; retinal disease can blindLarvae in tissue or serology; albendazole or mebendazole, though no proven treatment

The four drugs differ by mechanism, and each has its own set of worms. The mechanism of albendazole and mebendazole is to bind tubulin, block microtubule assembly, impair glucose uptake and deplete glycogen; they are used for pinworm, roundworm, hookworm and Toxocara, with albendazole for whipworm and cutaneous larva migrans. Pyrantel pamoate produces depolarizing neuromuscular blockade, contraction then paralysis, and the worm loses its grip; it is used for pinworm and hookworm. Ivermectin opens glutamate-gated chloride channels, with hyperpolarization, paralysis and death; it is used for Strongyloides (drug of choice) and is also effective for Ascaris and cutaneous larva migrans.

Points that carry questions
  • Before corticosteroids or TNF inhibitors in anyone from an endemic area, send Strongyloides serology and give ivermectin if positive; hyperinfection is strongly linked to HTLV-1 and corticosteroids, and also to malnutrition. Slide 71 lists AIDS, but HIV is only weakly associated.
  • Pinworm drugs kill adults but not eggs, so retreat at 2 weeks. Prolapse in Trichuris follows increased expulsive peristalsis.
  • The deck says human hookworms also cause cutaneous larva migrans and that Strongyloides does too; the dedicated slides key the animal Ancylostoma species, and human hookworms usually cause ground itch.
  • Prevention: proper sewage disposal, wearing shoes, hand washing and laundering bedding for pinworm.

7. Brucellosis and Non-inflammatory Diarrhea

Lecture scope: Lecture 6: Brucella (brucellosis) and non-inflammatory diarrhea or food poisoning organisms (Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, EHEC, ETEC and other diarrheagenic E. coli, Clostridium perfringens including gas gangrene): transmission, toxins, presentation, diagnosis, treatment.

Slide decks: Non-inflammatory Diarrhea and Toxin-mediated Enteric Infections (updated deck) (21 Qs) · Lect 6, Brucellosis, Non-inflammatory diarrhea (16 Qs)

The food-poisoning organisms are separated by time to onset, the food involved and the toxin: preformed toxin acts within hours, while toxins made in the gut act later. Onset in hours is intoxication, whereas 1 to 5 days is infection, in which bacteria had to colonize and make toxin. The toxins tip the balance toward secretion: raised cAMP or cGMP opens the CFTR channel, so chloride and water pour into the lumen, giving watery stool with no inflammation. Antimotility drugs are withheld when the stool is bloody or febrile, because they let an invasive organism such as Salmonella multiply (Class notes, non-inflammatory diarrhea, 10 Oct 2026).

Staphylococcus aureus and the emetic form of Bacillus cereus are clinically identical, so the food clue is used: potato salad is S. aureus and fried rice is B. cereus. Clostridium perfringens, a non-motile, encapsulated endospore-forming rod of soil and the human colon, reaches people in food or by traumatic implantation, and its alpha toxin (lecithinase) causes gas gangrene, which can become systemic within hours with hemolytic anemia, multi-organ failure and shock; it also has an enterotoxin that causes food poisoning after reheated meat. Among the diarrheagenic E. coli, ETEC gives the traveler's watery diarrhea with no blood, whereas EHEC O157:H7 gives bloody diarrhea with no fever and no pus, and antibiotics raise its HUS risk.

Brucella is a small aerobic Gram-negative coccobacillus that lives inside macrophages, spreads from domestic livestock through unpasteurized dairy or animal contact, and causes a relapsing fever with sweats, arthralgia and lymphadenopathy. Culture is hazardous, diagnosis uses serum agglutination, and rifampin plus doxycycline is given for at least 6 to 8 weeks.

High-Yield Notes

Incubation period is the clue to mechanism: hours means the toxin was in the food, days means bacteria had to colonize and make toxin. Watery stool, no fever and no blood: think toxin. Reheating kills the bacteria, not the toxin.

OrganismOnset and foodToxinIllness
Bacillus cereus, emetic form (motile, aerobic, spore-forming rod)1 to 6 h (earlier deck: 30 min to 6 h); rice (fried rice), pasta, sauces, soupsPreformed heat-stable enterotoxin, like S. aureus enterotoxinSevere vomiting; self-limiting within about 24 h
Bacillus cereus, diarrheal form8 to 18 h (earlier deck: 15 to 18 h); meat, vegetables, fishHeat-labile enterotoxin made after ingestion, like E. coli LTWatery diarrhea, cramps; self-limiting
Staphylococcus aureus (Gram-positive cocci in clusters)1 to 6 h (earlier deck: 30 min to 6 h); ham, custard, sliced meats, pastries, potato salad; food handler with nose or skin carriagePreformed enterotoxins A to E, fast acting, heat stableNausea, pain, vomiting, then diarrhea; no fever; supportive care only
Clostridium perfringens (Gram-positive, anaerobic, nonmotile, spore-forming rod)8 to 16 h (earlier deck: 6 to 24 h); reheated meat, gravy, raw meat and poultryHeat-labile enterotoxin binds small intestinal brush border, altering permeabilitySudden watery diarrhea and cramps, no fever; self-limiting

With an incubation of 1 to 6 h a preformed toxin is swallowed, no growth in the host needed (S. aureus, its enterotoxin preformed in food; B. cereus emetic); clinical clue: vomiting, everyone who shared the meal ill. At 8 to 18 h spores germinate, with toxin made in the gut (C. perfringens, 8 to 16 h; B. cereus diarrheal, 8 to 18 h): watery diarrhea, cramps, reheated meat. At 1 to 5 days comes colonization, then enterotoxin secretion (ETEC, 24 to 72 h; V. cholerae, section 9): travel, water, profuse watery stool.

The diarrheagenic E. coli share a Gram-negative rod, a lactose fermenter with a metallic green sheen on EMB agar, so the exam separates them by toxin and disease. Raised cAMP or cGMP opens the CFTR channel, so chloride and water pour into the lumen, giving watery stool with no inflammation. ETEC LT (heat-labile) has the same mechanism as cholera toxin: ADP-ribosylates Gs, raised cAMP, and ST (heat-stable) acts through guanylate cyclase, raised cGMP; each gives chloride and water secretion.

TypeSettingToxin and actionDisease and lab clue
EHEC O157:H7 (VTEC, STEC)Undercooked ground beef, raw milk, unpasteurized apple cider, contaminated leafy greens (safest produce is cooked, then washed); cattle and ruminants main carriersShiga-like toxin (verotoxin): B subunit binds Gb3, A subunit cleaves 28S rRNA in the 60S subunit and stops protein synthesisIncubation 3 to 8 days; bloody diarrhea, no fever, no pus; HUS (schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, kidney failure); antibiotics raise HUS risk; colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar
ETECFecal-oral via sewage, unwashed utensils or hands; travelers (Montezuma's revenge)LT: raised cAMP. ST: raised cGMP.Watery diarrhea, no blood, no WBCs; onset 24 to 72 h; 3 to 5 days, self-limited
EPECInfantsAttaches and effaces microvilli (intimin, Tir)Infant watery diarrhea
EIECMimics ShigellaInvades colonic epitheliumDysentery, fever (inflammatory)
EAECTravelersNot statedAnother cause of traveler's diarrhea (after ETEC)
DAECNot statedNot statedNot stated

Brucellosis is Brucella melitensis (goats, sheep) B. abortus (cattle), B. suis (swine) and B. canis (dogs), a Gram-negative coccobacillus, capnophilic, facultative intracellular, with endotoxin, reticuloendothelial spread and granulomas with central necrosis. Diagnosis: culture is hazardous; serum agglutination with fourfold titer rise or antibody above 160. Treatment and prevention: rifampin plus doxycycline for at least 6 to 8 weeks; pasteurize milk, vaccinate cattle.

Traveler's diarrhea has ETEC as most common cause (others EAEC, Campylobacter, Shigella, norovirus), fecal-oral via food and water. Diagnosis: stool shows no white cells. Treatment and prevention: rehydrate (ORS, IV if severe); antibiotics only if severe (azithromycin or fluoroquinolone); loperamide only if no fever and no blood; safe food and water, hand washing.

Gas gangrene (myonecrosis) is C. perfringens spores germinating anaerobically in a wound; the alpha toxin (phospholipase C, lecithinase) damages membranes and causes hemolysis; atherosclerosis, colon cancer and diabetes predispose. Diagnosis: Nagler reaction on egg-yolk agar, double zone of hemolysis on blood agar; nonmotile. Treatment and prevention: extensive debridement with delayed closure, penicillin G, clindamycin if penicillin allergic, hyperbaric oxygen.

Points that carry questions
  • Brucellosis is an occupational disease of ranchers, dairy farmers, abattoir workers and veterinarians, and Brucella is a potential biowarfare agent.
  • Initial management of acute watery diarrhea: assess dehydration, replace with ORS if mild to moderate or IV fluid if severe, monitor urine output, potassium and bicarbonate, keep feeding, and avoid antimotility drugs if bloody or febrile. Fluids first, antibiotics second.
  • Buzzwords: potato salad, 4 h is S. aureus; fried rice, vomiting is B. cereus; reheated meat is C. perfringens; traveler, watery is ETEC; incubation 1 to 6 h is preformed toxin; oysters with cirrhosis and raw fish in Japan are Vibrio (section 9).
  • Onset windows overlap (earlier deck: ETEC 12 to 72 h), so use the food history. Unsafe food temperature is 40 F to 140 F; refrigerate within 2 hours.

8. Viral Hepatitis

Lecture scope: Lectures 7a and 7b: hepatitis A, B, C, D and E viruses (genome and structure, transmission, pathogenesis, clinical features, HBV serology and mutants, HCV antibody versus RNA, HDV co-infection versus superinfection, histology, treatment and prevention), plus yellow fever, EBV, CMV and other viruses that cause hepatitis.

Slide decks: Viral Hepatitis I, HBV, HCV, HDV (updated deck) (33 Qs) · Viral Hepatitis II, HAV, HEV, Yellow Fever (updated deck) (21 Qs) · Lect 7, Viral Hepatitis (27 Qs)

Five unrelated viruses cause viral hepatitis, separated by genome, route and chronicity: hepatitis A and E are fecal-oral RNA viruses that never (or rarely) become chronic, whereas B, C and D spread by blood, sex and birth and can persist. Parenteral exposure includes shared needles, needlesticks, tattooing and piercing and shared razors or toothbrushes. About 75% of chronic HBV carriers live in Asia and the Western Pacific rim, and about one third of chronic carriers have chronic active hepatitis that can end in cirrhosis, liver failure or hepatocellular carcinoma, whereas alcoholism greatly enhances the carcinoma rate in HCV. Raw shellfish also carries norovirus, which gives vomiting and diarrhea without jaundice, whereas hepatitis A gives jaundice (Class notes, Viral Hepatitis II, 8 Oct 2026). Hepatitis A has only uncommon relapsing, fulminant or cholestatic complications. Clinically they look alike: a prodrome of fever, fatigue and nausea, then dark urine, clay-colored stool, jaundice and tender hepatomegaly with ALT higher than AST, and the injury is immune mediated, by CD8+ T cells attacking infected hepatocytes.

The most tested block is the HBV serologic panel: HBsAg rises first, IgM anti-HBc marks recent infection and fills the window period, and anti-HBs protects. Delta depends on timing relative to HBV, read here as setting, then course and marker. In HDV co-infection HBV and HDV are acquired together: more severe acute hepatitis, chronic rare, IgM anti-HBc positive. HDV superinfection is HDV in a chronic HBsAg carrier: it replicates at once and is more severe, with cirrhosis risk, chronic common, mortality above 20%, and IgG anti-HBc plus new anti-HDV.

HCV is antibody plus RNA. Anti-HCV positive, RNA positive is the acute or chronic pattern, an active replicating infection; treat with DAAs. Anti-HCV negative, RNA positive is very early acute: RNA appears before antibody. Anti-HCV positive, RNA negative is cleared or treated: past infection; antibody is not protective. Yellow fever is the classic severe hemorrhagic hepatitis, while EBV and CMV cause milder transaminitis, separated by the heterophile antibody.

High-Yield Notes

Five viruses compared: read the table one virus at a time, from family and genome through transmission and incubation to severity and chronicity. Deck conflicts: HBV incubation 45 to 160 days or 4 to 26 weeks; HCV chronic 80% or 70% (keep 80%).

Treatment and prevention, by use, with the deck point. Chronic HBV: tenofovir, entecavir, lamivudine, nucleoside analogs that block HBV RT; the YMDD mutation (P gene) gives lamivudine resistance. Also chronic HBV: pegylated IFN-alpha 2a, IFN-alpha conjugated with polyethylene glycol. HCV: glecaprevir plus pibrentasvir; sofosbuvir plus velpatasvir, DAAs, all six genotypes; sofosbuvir plus ledipasvir, genotypes 1, 4, 5 and 6 only; interferon plus ribavirin, preferred before DAAs.

HEV: reduce immunosuppression, ribavirin; HEV239 vaccine. Chronic genotype 3 in transplant recipients; HEV239 licensed in China only. HAV: inactivated HAV vaccine; immune globulin. Two doses 6 months apart; postexposure within 2 weeks. HBV, and HDV by extension: recombinant HBsAg vaccine; HBIG. Doses at 0, 1 and 6 months; vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours of birth for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers and after needlestick.

Key points
  • Fulminant hepatitis: small, shrunken, soft liver.
  • HDV replicates in the nucleus (deck: cytoplasm).
  • HBV genes: S (HBsAg), C (pre-C makes HBeAg; HBcAg stays intracellular, never free in blood), X (HBxAg, binds p53), P (polymerase with RT). Precore mutants lack HBeAg yet replicate and progress faster; escape mutants (S gene) defeat vaccine and HBIG.
  • Biopsy clues: Councilman bodies (apoptotic, acidophil; HAV, yellow fever), ground glass (HBV, HBsAg in ER), lymphoid aggregates (HCV).
  • Anti-HAV IgM is diagnostic of HAV; IgG marks immunity.
  • HBV: over 90% of adults recover; over 90% of newborns become chronic.
  • HBV immune complexes cause rash, polyarthritis, polyarteritis nodosum and glomerulonephritis.
  • HCV mutates E2 (no proofreading), so there is no vaccine (six genotypes); it is the leading cause of US liver transplantation. NS3/NS4A blunts interferon. Biopsy: portal lymphoid aggregates, interface hepatitis, steatosis. Extrahepatic: diabetes, glomerulonephritis, mixed cryoglobulinemia, porphyria cutanea tarda, NHL.
  • HDV causes 40% of fulminant hepatitis, fatal in up to 80%; delta antigen is acute, anti-HDV chronic.

9. Vibrio Species

Lecture scope: Lecture 8: Vibrio cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus as non-inflammatory or invasive seafood and water-borne pathogens: morphology, transmission, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

Slide decks: Lect 8, Vibrio cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus, V. vulnificus (9 Qs) · SGD, Vibrio (5 Qs) · Non-inflammatory Diarrhea and Toxin-mediated Enteric Infections (updated deck) (2 Qs)

The Vibrio species are curved, comma-shaped, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods acquired from contaminated water or seafood. They split into a toxin-driven, non-invasive diarrhea (V. cholerae), a self-limited enterotoxin diarrhea from raw seafood (V. parahaemolyticus) and a wound or septicemic infection of high-risk hosts (V. vulnificus), separated by culture color on TCBS agar, salt tolerance, host and clinical picture.

On TCBS agar, V. cholerae ferments sucrose and grows as yellow colonies, whereas V. parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus do not ferment sucrose and grow as blue-green colonies. Growth conditions then set V. cholerae apart: it is alkalinophilic and does not grow in 8% NaCl, whereas V. parahaemolyticus is a halophilic marine organism that grows in 8% NaCl, and V. vulnificus is likewise a halophilic marine organism.

Host and clinical picture do the rest. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha, raising adenylate cyclase and cAMP and opening CFTR for chloride secretion, and the illness is abrupt watery diarrhea with rice-water stool, managed by prompt water and electrolyte replacement with tetracyclines optional. V. parahaemolyticus follows raw fish or shellfish and is self-limited for about 3 days. V. vulnificus causes wound infection with hemorrhagic bullae after wound exposure, or primary septicemia within 24 hours, and its high-risk hosts are those with liver disease or hemochromatosis.

High-Yield Notes

Read the first table one organism at a time, across source and transmission, illness, and treatment and prevention. The illness column carries the incubation period and the approximate fatality figures where the deck gives them, along with the stool or wound picture, with the slide named beside several of the figures. In the last column, V. cholerae and V. vulnificus have a named treatment, while V. parahaemolyticus is not stated as needing antibiotics and is given prevention measures.

Other traveler's diarrhea bacteria are named beside Vibrio on the lecture slide, with the following deck detail. About 50% of traveler's diarrhea cases are ETEC. Inflammatory bloody diarrhea localized to the colon and jejunum is the picture of Campylobacter jejuni, which is treated with antibiotics, in contrast to V. cholerae (toxigenic watery diarrhea of the small intestine, fluid replacement) (slide 3). Salmonella and Shigella are listed only as traveler's diarrhea causes, with no features stated.

Points that carry questions
  • V. cholerae O1 has classic and El Tor biotypes and Ogawa, Inaba and Hikojima serotypes; darting "shooting star" motility from a single polar flagellum.
  • V. cholerae needs a high infectious dose (more than 10 to the 7) because it is acid-sensitive; antacids lower the dose and blood group O has more severe disease (non-inflammatory diarrhea deck, slide 27; Class notes, cholera and Vibrio, 10 Oct 2026).
  • Cholera toxin is an A-B5 toxin: the five B subunits bind GM1 ganglioside; stool is enriched in alkaline peptone water before TCBS agar (non-inflammatory diarrhea deck, slides 29 and 30).
  • V. vulnificus is the leading cause of shellfish-associated deaths in the United States.
  • Suspected cholera is treated before laboratory confirmation because death from dehydration can occur within hours; the serum abnormalities are hypokalemia and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss (non-inflammatory diarrhea deck, slide 28).

10. Inflammatory Diarrhea: Campylobacter, C. difficile, Yersinia

Lecture scope: Lecture 9: C. difficile, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica as causes of inflammatory diarrhea: morphology, risk groups, transmission, pathogenesis, clinical syndromes, complications, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

Slide decks: Lect 9, Inflammatory diarrhea (12 Qs) · SGD, C. difficile, Campylobacter, Yersinia (10 Qs) · SGD, C. difficile, Campylobacter, Yersinia (pre-reading) (1 Q)

Inflammatory diarrhea comes from invasion or cytotoxin damage of the mucosa: fever, cramping pain and bloody or purulent stool with fecal leukocytes. In a toxigenic infection the microbe stays on the surface of epithelial cells and secretes toxin into the cells, disrupting cell metabolism with loss of water and electrolytes and a watery stool. In an invasive infection it destroys epithelial cells and forms ulcerations, with loss of the intestinal lining and bleeding, with fever.

Three organisms are covered: Clostridioides difficile, an anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive rod that follows antibiotic use; Campylobacter jejuni, a microaerophilic curved rod acquired mainly from poultry; and Yersinia enterocolitica, a Gram-negative rod from pork that grows in the cold. In C. difficile, antibiotics destroy normal colonic flora, allowing overgrowth; toxin A is an enterotoxin and toxin B is a cytotoxin, and the picture is watery, occasionally bloody diarrhea with fever and pseudomembranes.

Both Campylobacter and Yersinia can mimic appendicitis, so pork and cold enrichment point to Yersinia, poultry and 42°C to Campylobacter. Reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum follow both Campylobacter and Yersinia infection, whereas GBS is specific to Campylobacter in this lecture.

High-Yield Notes

The table sorts every diarrheal organism in sections 7, 9, 10 and 11 by how it causes disease. Read a row from what the microbe does to the result, then to the organisms listed with that mechanism and their section.

MechanismWhat the microbe doesResultOrganisms
Preformed toxinToxin is already in the food when it is eatenVomiting within 30 min to 6 hBacillus cereus emetic form, Staphylococcus aureus (section 7)
Toxigenic infectionStays on the surface of epithelial cells and secretes toxin into the cellsDisrupted cell metabolism with loss of water and electrolytes: watery stoolETEC, B. cereus diarrheal form, Clostridium perfringens (section 7); Vibrio cholerae, and V. parahaemolyticus, where limited invasion can add blood and fever (section 9)
CytotoxinToxin damages the epithelium itselfEHEC: bloody stool with no fever, no pus. C. difficile: watery, occasionally bloody, with fever and pseudomembranesEHEC, Shiga-like toxin (section 7); C. difficile, toxin B (this section)
Invasive infectionDestroys epithelial cells and forms ulcerationsLoss of the intestinal lining and bleeding, with feverCampylobacter jejuni, and Yersinia enterocolitica, which gives blood and pus although the deck names only its enterotoxin (this section); Salmonella gastroenteritis, and Shigella, with Shiga toxin added in S. dysenteriae (section 11)
Invasion with spreadCrosses the gut lining, is engulfed by macrophages and replicates in liver, spleen and bone marrowGradually rising fever and rose spots after 10 to 14 days; diarrhea or constipationSalmonella Typhi, enteric fever (section 11)

C. difficile is an anaerobic, Gram-positive, endospore-forming rod. Its source is endogenous (colonized carriers) and nosocomial spore spread (surfaces); slide 3 words the source as endogenous only, but slide 7 advises isolating symptomatic patients and disinfecting contaminated surfaces. It colonizes about 3% of the general population and up to 30% of hospitalized patients; risk is recent antibiotics (clindamycin, ampicillin, amoxicillin, cephalosporins, ciprofloxacin), proton pump inhibitor use, a hospital or nursing-home stay, age 65 or over. In pathogenesis, antibiotics destroy normal colonic flora, allowing overgrowth; toxin A is an enterotoxin binding the brush border, toxin B is a cytotoxin that disrupts the actin cytoskeleton, raising permeability and causing apoptosis. Symptoms begin within days of antibiotics: watery diarrhea (occasionally bloody), yellow-white mucosal plaques (pseudomembranes), nausea, fever, cramps, loss of appetite. Toxic megacolon and colonic perforation are the complications.

Campylobacter jejuni is microaerophilic and grows at 42°C; a Gram-negative comma or S-shaped, motile rod; oxidase and catalase positive. Its source is fecal-oral, mainly poultry; also unpasteurized milk, contaminated water, and puppies or kittens with diarrhea (common for children); as few as 500 organisms cause disease; the commonest bacterial enteric pathogen in high-income countries. Pathogenesis is mucosal invasion with bloody diarrhea; reservoirs are cattle, chickens, sheep, cats and dogs. Incubation 1 to 8 days; ten or more watery stools a day, fever, cramps, nausea, vomiting; bloody stool in 15% of adults and over 50% of children; traveler's diarrhea; pseudoappendicitis; usually self-limiting. Late complications are reactive arthritis (mainly HLA-B27), Guillain-Barré syndrome by molecular mimicry between C. jejuni lipopolysaccharide and myelin (under 0.1% of infections, yet up to 40% of GBS cases follow documented infection in the prior 2 weeks), erythema nodosum.

Yersinia enterocolitica (Enterobacteriaceae) is a Gram-negative facultative rod, oxidase negative, non-lactose fermenter, non-H2S producer; motile at 25°C but not at 37°C. Source and risk: pigs are the major reservoir; raw or undercooked pork, pet feces (puppies), unpasteurized milk or untreated water; day-care outbreaks; commoner in cold months. In pathogenesis, it grows at refrigerator temperature; enterotoxin similar in action to the ETEC heat-stable toxin. Onset 4 to 7 days after exposure; young children have fever, abdominal pain and bloody, purulent diarrhea; older children and adults have fever and right lower quadrant pain that mimics appendicitis. Complications are reactive arthritis about 1 month later and erythema nodosum.

The table compares the same organisms by laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention. Read down the diagnosis column first: toxins in stool for C. difficile, a named agar each for Campylobacter and Yersinia.

OrganismDiagnosisTreatmentPrevention
C. difficileDetection of enterotoxin and cytotoxin in stoolStop the precipitating antibiotic; fluids; oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin (inhibits RNA polymerase); oral metronidazole only if those are unavailable; fecal microbiota transplant when medical therapy fails in recurrent casesAvoid overprescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics; isolate symptomatic patients; disinfect contaminated surfaces
Campylobacter jejuniSkirrow agar (blood agar with vancomycin, trimethoprim and polymyxin B), incubated at 42°C in 5% oxygen and 10% CO2Fluid and electrolyte replacement; antibiotics generally not required; azithromycin or ciprofloxacin if severe or complicatedThorough cooking, pasteurization of milk, disinfecting surfaces used for raw meat
Yersinia enterocoliticaCIN agar is the selective medium; cold enrichment at 4°C for 24 to 48 hoursSupportive care; aminoglycosides, cephalosporins or TMP-SMX for severe or complicated infectionProper handling and cooking of meat; clean cutting boards after raw meat
Points that carry questions
  • Pseudoappendicitis is the shared mimic: both Campylobacter and Yersinia can mimic appendicitis, so pork and cold enrichment point to Yersinia, poultry and 42°C to Campylobacter.
  • Reactive arthritis and erythema nodosum follow both Campylobacter and Yersinia infection; GBS is specific to Campylobacter in this lecture.
  • The SGD pre-reading frames the topic as inflammatory (invasive or cytotoxin damage, fecal leukocytes) versus secretory diarrhea.

11. Inflammatory Diarrhea: Salmonella and Shigella

Lecture scope: Lecture 10: Salmonella (gastroenteritis, septicemia, enteric fever, carriage) and Shigella (bacillary dysentery, Shiga toxin, HUS): transmission, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

Slide decks: Lect 10, Inflammatory diarrhea (16 Qs) · SGD, Salmonella, Shigella (5 Qs) · SGD, Salmonella, Shigella (pre-reading) (0 Qs)

Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative Enterobacteriaceae that invade the intestinal mucosa through M cells. Salmonella survives inside macrophages and can cause septicemia or enteric fever; Shigella spreads cell to cell on actin, rarely reaches the blood, and one species makes Shiga toxin. The Shigella illness is bacillary dysentery, with tenesmus and watery then bloody diarrhea, and the renal damage of Shiga toxin causes HUS.

Salmonella is motile, makes H2S, needs a high dose and has animal reservoirs (except S. Typhi), whereas Shigella is non-motile, makes no H2S, needs a very low dose and lives only in humans. On Hektoen enteric agar Salmonella is green with black centers while E. coli is orange-yellow, and on MacConkey agar Salmonella enterica and Shigella are non-lactose fermenters.

Salmonella infection takes four forms. Gastroenteritis, from S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis, is the most common form in the US and has an incubation of 6 to 48 hours, whereas enteric fever begins 10 to 14 days after ingestion with a gradually rising fever and rose spots. Septicemia is more common in sickle cell disease, where Salmonella is the most common cause of osteomyelitis, and in asymptomatic colonization S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi survive in the gallbladder.

High-Yield Notes

The table sets the four forms of Salmonella infection side by side. Read across a row for the organisms and source, then the clinical picture and the treatment where one is stated; the third column also carries timing where given.

SepticemiaS. Typhi, Paratyphi, Choleraesuis, DublinGram-negative septicemia; osteomyelitis, endocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia; more common in sickle cell disease, cancer, or a child with enterocolitis; most common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell diseaseFluoroquinolones or third-generation cephalosporins for severe disease

Paratyphi A and B are inferred to cause it too from their Widal antigens (slide 15); strictly human; food handlers, contaminated food or water; low infectious dose, so person-to-person spread is common10 to 14 days after ingestion: gradually rising fever, rose spots on trunk and abdomen, headache, weakness, anorexia, abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation; GI symptoms in week 3; intestinal ulceration and perforation; suspect in febrile travelers from endemic areasFluoroquinolones or third-generation cephalosporins; vaccines below
Asymptomatic colonizationS. Typhi and S. ParatyphiSurvive in the gallbladder; carriage for more than 1 year after disease in 1% to 5%Not stated

Salmonella is a motile, H2S producer with an animal reservoir (poultry, eggs, dairy, reptiles); S. Typhi is human only. Infectious dose is high, 10^6 to 10^8; lower gastric acidity is a risk factor. Host risk groups are children under 5, adults over 60, leukemia, lymphoma, sickle cell disease. It invades through M cells of Peyer patches in endocytic vacuoles, survives in macrophages by reduced phagosome-lysosome fusion, and can reach blood and lymph. Incubation is 6 to 48 hours (gastroenteritis) or 10 to 14 days (enteric fever). Complications are reactive arthritis, and osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease; treatment is fluoroquinolones or third-generation cephalosporins (severe, typhoid).

Shigella is non-motile, no H2S; its reservoir is humans only, spread by fingers, flies, food, feces. Infectious dose is low; extremely acid resistant. Host risk is primarily pediatric: 60% of infections under 10 years. It invades through M cells, then the cytoplasm, with actin jet trails and very shallow ulcers, and rarely invades vessels or causes septicemia. Incubation is 1 to 4 days, then bacillary dysentery: fever above 38.3 C, lower abdominal cramps, tenesmus, watery then bloody diarrhea. Complications are HUS, reactive arthritis, seizures, peritonitis; treatment is fluids; severe cases get ciprofloxacin and azithromycin to shorten illness in children.

S. sonnei is the most common Shigella in the US, S. flexneri and S. boydii are named only in the deck, with no further features stated, and S. dysenteriae has the most severe disease; type 1 makes Shiga toxin. The Enterobacteriaceae lactose fermenters are E. coli, Citrobacter, Klebsiella, Enterobacter; the non-lactose fermenters (ShYPS) are Shigella, Yersinia, Proteus, Salmonella; motile H2S producers are Salmonella and Proteus; non-H2S producers are Shigella and Yersinia (slide 3 lists both as non-motile; Shigella is non-motile, but Yersinia is motile at 25 C and not at 37 C). Shared features of the Enterobacteriaceae: Gram-negative rods, facultative anaerobes, ferment glucose, oxidase negative, reduce nitrate to nitrite, catalase positive.

Culture blood, bone marrow, CSF, urine, a rectal swab or other sites. In week 1, 80% of blood cultures are positive and 25% of patients have rose spots; by week 3, 85% of stool cultures are positive; a rose spot can also be biopsied. On MacConkey agar, E. coli ferments lactose; Salmonella enterica and Shigella are lac- (non-lactose fermenters). Bismuth sulfite agar is selective for Salmonella; on Hektoen enteric agar Salmonella gives green colonies with black centers while E. coli is orange-yellow with bile precipitates.

The Widal test is presumptive: an O titer above 160 means active infection and an H titer above 160 means past infection; Paratyphi A and B carry the AH and BH flagellar antigens. The typhoid vaccines are live attenuated Ty21a, given orally, and the ViCPS capsular polysaccharide, given parenterally.

Shiga toxin of S. dysenteriae type 1 binds Gb3 through its B subunit, and its A subunit cleaves the 28S rRNA of the 60S subunit; it is enterotoxic, cytotoxic and neurotoxic, and renal damage causes HUS. The EHEC Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin) is a phage-encoded exotoxin with the same 60S mechanism and the same HUS. Shigella is prevented by sewage control, clean drinking water and hand washing; Salmonella by cooking food and washing hands.

Points that carry questions
  • Deck slide 22 lists Shiga toxin among the phage-encoded ABCDE exotoxins; the S. dysenteriae toxin gene is chromosomal, and it is EHEC Shiga-like toxin that is phage-encoded, so key that version.
  • Yersinia appears in this deck only as a non-lactose fermenter and non-H2S producer, and slide 3 lists it as non-motile; the standard fact, taught in the previous lecture, is that it is motile at 25 C but not at 37 C.
  • Salmonella is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease.
